analysis.one_liner: Overhauls health insurance: bans coverage denials for preexisting conditions and extends subsidized coverage to millions.
analysis.headline: Became law on March 23, 2010 after the Senate passed it 60-39 and the House agreed to the Senate version 219-212.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill overhauled the American health insurance system. It bans insurers from denying coverage or charging more to people with preexisting conditions, stops insurers from canceling policies when someone gets sick, and ends annual and lifetime dollar caps on benefits. It expands Medicaid to people earning up to 133% of the poverty line and gives refundable tax credits to people earning up to 400% of poverty to help buy coverage. It also requires nearly everyone to carry insurance or pay a penalty, and it raises revenue through taxes on high earners and annual fees on insurers, brand-name drug makers, and medical device makers.
analysis.who_benefits: The uninsured and underinsured gain the most: people with preexisting conditions can no longer be denied coverage, low-income people gain Medicaid eligibility, households earning up to four times the poverty line get premium tax credits and reduced out-of-pocket costs, young adults can stay on a parent's plan until age 26, and everyone gets free preventive care. Small businesses with up to 25 employees get a tax credit for half their health coverage costs. Insurers, drug makers, and hospitals also gain from tens of millions of newly insured, paying customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured Americans and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Insurers may no longer deny coverage or set eligibility rules based on health status, and premiums may vary only by coverage type, rating area, age, and tobacco use.

Medicaid expands to people under 65 with incomes at or below 133% of the poverty line beginning in 2014, with the federal government paying 100% of the cost of covering newly eligible people from 2014 to 2016.
Households earning between 100% and 400% of the poverty line receive a refundable tax credit for a percentage of their health plan premiums, plus reduced out-of-pocket limits.
Health plans must cover adult children up to age 26, cover preventive services with no cost sharing, and cannot cancel coverage except for fraud.

Insurers can no longer set annual or lifetime dollar limits on benefits, must justify premium increases publicly, and must rebate premium revenue they do not spend on medical care (85% minimum for large group plans, 80% for small group and individual plans).
Qualified small employers with up to 25 workers can claim a tax credit for 50% of their employee health coverage costs.
A temporary high-risk insurance pool was created immediately for people with preexisting conditions who had been uninsured for six months, until the main provisions take effect in 2014.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals earning over $200,000 (or couples over $250,000) pay a 0.9% higher Medicare payroll tax, and high-income Medicare enrollees pay higher Part D premiums. Health insurers, brand-name drug manufacturers, and medical device makers pay new annual fees on their sales. Employers with more than 50 full-time workers face fines if they do not offer affordable coverage or if enrollment waits exceed 60 days. Hospitals absorb Medicare payment reductions and cuts to uncompensated-care payments. People who remain uninsured pay a penalty on their taxes. Some costs may be passed to consumers through premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, insurers, drug and device makers, large employers

drawbacks.text: Beginning in 2014, almost everyone must maintain health coverage or pay a penalty, forcing people who would rather go uninsured to buy a commercial policy or pay the government.

The bill creates no government-run public plan; instead, it requires people to buy coverage from private insurers, and the grandfather rule exempts plans already in existence from most of the new consumer protections.
Premium rates may still vary by age by a factor of up to 4 to 1, so older adults can be charged several times what young adults pay for the same coverage.
Brand-name biologic drugs get 12 years of market exclusivity before cheaper copies can be approved, delaying lower-cost alternatives.
Federal funds may not be used for abortion services, and states may ban abortion coverage entirely in plans sold on the exchanges.

The Senate-passed version included a provision directing the federal government to pay 100% of the cost of covering newly eligible Medicaid recipients in Nebraska from 2017 onward, a carve-out for a single state that drew wide criticism.

Costs imposed on insurers, drug makers, and device makers may be passed through to consumers in premiums and prices; an honest supporter must acknowledge the bill works through the same private industries it regulates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for ordinary people are large and concrete: preexisting condition protections, a major Medicaid expansion, and subsidies that make coverage affordable for millions who previously could not buy it. The costs are real but mostly fall on concentrated groups: high earners, large employers, and health industries. The main structural weakness is that the bill channels the mandate and the subsidies through private insurers rather than a public plan, which locks those companies into a guaranteed customer base while capping their overhead. The single-state Medicaid carve-out in the Senate version was an unnecessary blemish that fed public distrust even as the core provisions protected consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The House first passed it 416-0 as a narrow military homebuyer tax bill; the Senate rewrote it into the full health care law, passed it 60-39 on December 24, 2009, and the House then agreed to the Senate amendments 219-212 on March 21, 2010, with President Obama signing it two days later.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 17, 2009 as the Service Members Home Ownership Tax Act of 2009, a narrow tax bill extending the first-time homebuyer credit for service members on extended duty abroad.

The House passed that version without amendment on October 8, 2009 under suspension of the rules, a procedure reserved for non-controversial bills that requires a two-thirds majority, by a vote of 416-0 with every Democrat and Republican voting yes.

The Senate then replaced the bill's contents with the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. It needed 60 votes just to proceed to debate, which it got on November 21, 2009 by 60-39, with every voting Democrat and independent in favor and every Republican opposed.

During three weeks of Senate debate, Republican senators McCain, Hatch, Johanns, Crapo, and Hutchison repeatedly offered motions to send the bill back to the Finance Committee with instructions; every one failed, with votes ranging from 41-58 to 45-54.
The Senate passed the bill on December 24, 2009 by 60-39, the exact minimum needed, with all 58 voting Democrats plus two independents in favor and all 39 voting Republicans opposed.

Because the Senate had amended the House bill, the House had to vote again. On March 21, 2010 it agreed to the Senate amendments 219-212, with no Republican support, 219 Democrats in favor, and 34 Democrats joining all 178 Republicans in opposition.
President Obama signed the bill on March 23, 2010, making it Public Law 111-148.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who were uninsured or had preexisting conditions gained enforceable protections and subsidized coverage, and the private health insurance industry gained a guaranteed pool of mandated, subsidized customers with its central role locked into law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The uninsured, and insurers whose role was locked in

sides.party_line_note: The bill was almost entirely a Democratic project: in the Senate, 58 Democrats plus 2 independents passed it 60-39 over unanimous Republican opposition, and in the House all 178 Republicans and 34 of 253 Democrats voted no on final passage, leaving only Democratic votes for the law.

industries.note: The bill forbids denying coverage to people with preexisting conditions, ends lifetime dollar caps and policy rescissions, and caps overhead by requiring rebates when insurers spend too little of premiums on care (85% for large-group plans, 80% for small-group and individual plans). At the same time, the individual mandate routes millions of new, partly subsidized customers to these same private companies, and the bill creates no public competitor, making their gatekeeper role permanent.

Drug makers pay a new annual fee on branded drug sales, larger Medicaid rebates, and discounts for seniors in the Medicare coverage gap. In exchange, the bill grants them 12 years of market exclusivity for biologic drugs before cheaper biosimilars can be approved, delaying lower-cost competition for patients.

Individuals earning over $200,000 and couples over $250,000 pay a 0.9% higher Medicare payroll tax, high-income Medicare enrollees pay more for Part D, and health insurance executives face a $500,000 cap on the tax deductibility of their compensation.
Device manufacturers and importers pay an annual fee on gross sales above $5 million, a cost they may pass through in device prices.

Hospitals gain millions of newly insured patients who can pay their bills, but absorb Medicare payment reductions (productivity-adjusted updates), cuts to uncompensated-care payments as more people gain coverage, and a requirement to publish standard charges.

Employers with more than 50 full-time workers face fines if they fail to offer affordable coverage or impose long waiting periods; those that already provide coverage face little change, and small employers instead get a 50% tax credit.

The bill blocks physician-owned hospitals without an existing Medicare agreement from participating in Medicare, limiting doctors' ability to profit by referring patients to hospitals they own, though rural exceptions apply.
A 10% excise tax applies to indoor tanning services starting July 1, 2010.
